To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
amiloride inhibits responses to NaCl in Type I taste cells of the mouse fungiform taste bud.
amiloride inhibits fungiform taste buds by acting on amiloride-sensitive channels located in taste cells that have voltage-gated inward Na+ currents.
the principal finding of this study is that amilorid-sensitive sodium channels are expressed in taste cells that lack voltage gated inward currents, likely type I taste cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular mechanisms of taste perception.
the cellular mechanisms underlying salt taste.
the molecular basis of taste sensation and the mechanisms by which taste stimuli are transduced to nerve impulses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Type I taste cell is a candidate cell type for amiloride-sensitive salt taste transduction.
ENaCs in fungiform taste cells are expressed in Type I cells, and not Type II or Type III cells.
the taste cells expressing amiloride-sensitive channels are Type I taste cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Type I cells in fungiform taste buds express amiloride-sensitive ENaCs, whereas Type II cells express PLC signalling components.
the Type I cells of fungiform taste buds are the principal cells that mediate Na+ transduction, and the Type II cells are the principal cells mediating bitter, sweet and umami transduction.
Type I taste cells in fungiform taste buds are the primary site of Na+ salt transductions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amiloride-sensitive channels are not expressed by Type II or III cells, but are instead expressed by Type I cells.
Type I cells, in addition to their support functions, are the cells responsible for Na+ salt transductions in fungiform taste buds of mice.
amiloridesensitive Na+ channels are expressed in Type I cells, and not Type II cells, as has been widely presumed.
